parts.name: Arrival
parts.stand: On the main cobbled lane, Nikolaou Nomikou, at a spot where you can step aside and see over the caldera.

paras.t: Welcome to Oia, at the northwestern tip of Santorini. This cobbled lane is its main street, Nikolaou Nomikou.
The lanes are narrow and crowded, and the walls above the drops are low. Step aside when you stop, and keep children close.
The lane winds along the rim of the caldera. Oia has a nickname, the Eagle's Nest. Out over the water you can see the two volcanic islands, Palia and Nea Kameni, and the island of Therasia.

The name itself has wandered. For centuries this place was called Apano Meria, the upper side. It only became Oia in the later 1800s. The ancient Oia was somewhere else entirely, a harbor in the southeast of the island, where Kamari is now.

parts.name: The captains' village
parts.stand: Keep walking along the lane toward the higher part of the village, and stop where the larger, grander houses begin.

paras.t: Oia was a sailors' town. In the late 1800s its merchant ships traded across the eastern Mediterranean, from Alexandria to Russia.

In 1890 it had about 2,500 people and about 130 sailing ships. The wealthy captains built themselves neo-classical mansions, and their two-story houses up on the highest part of the village are still a reminder of that money.

One of those mansions, a block back from the cliff-top, is now the maritime museum. Inside are ship figureheads, sailors' sea chests and models of island ships. And it wasn't only ships: fine wine from the farmland behind the village went out to France and beyond.
Then the world changed. Steamships came, shipping gathered at Piraeus near Athens, and Oia's sea trade collapsed.
In the early 1900s wars, economic depression and overfishing hit the town too. And people moved away, many of them to Piraeus.

parts.name: Earthquake and rebirth
parts.stand: Find a place along the lane where you can look down at the houses dug into the cliff below.

paras.t: In 1956 an earthquake destroyed part of the town. At Oia, parts of the ground fell into the sea.
People left. By 1977 Oia had only 306 inhabitants. Imagine these lanes nearly empty.

But help was already on its way. In 1976, Oia was taken into a program of the Greek National Tourism Organisation to preserve traditional villages, under Aris Konstantinidis. The simple seamen's houses on the cliff edge became guest houses, hotels and restaurants. The work won the Europa Nostra Prize in 1979.
And the visitors came. Oia became known as a picture-perfect town, crowded every summer. Filmmakers noticed as well: Oia was the center of the story in the 1982 film Summer Lovers.

parts.name: Cave houses and white walls
parts.stand: Stay looking down at the cliff houses.

paras.t: Look at the houses below you, carved into the cliff. The pumice around them is full of air, so they stay warm in winter and cool in summer.

Many of these cave houses were homes for the ships' crews. And why so white? Explanations differ. One is practical: lime wash helps rainwater run off the roofs to be collected. Another is simply that it looks beautiful. And there's a story that under Ottoman rule Greeks couldn't fly their flag, so in Oia they painted the whole town white in defiance.
Notice the churches too. Oia has many restored churches, including the Panagia church. Some were built in memory of sailors.

parts.name: The castle and the sunset
parts.stand: Walk to the end of the village, near the ruined castle, and find a spot facing west over the water.

paras.t: This is Oia's ruined castle, Fort Londsa, a lookout over the whole caldera.

It was part of the same Venetian defense system as the castle at Pyrgos, and once one of the strongest fortresses on the island. The Venetian age here began in 1207, when Marco Sanudo founded the Duchy of Naxos, and Oia was home to one of the island's five local citadels.
Look for the old windmill too. It's one of the most recognizable buildings in Oia, and it turns up on a lot of postcards.

North of the castle, steep stairs lead down to the little harbor of Ammoudi, about 300 steps. It's a long way back up, so save your legs if the day is hot, and carry water. The sun here is strong, and dehydration and sunburn are the island's most common health problems.
Down at Ammoudi there are a few tavernas and a pebble beach, right on the water.
And at sunset, all of Oia fills with people. For a few seconds, the white houses and the whole caldera catch the colors of the setting sun.

parts.name: Closing
parts.stand: Stay where you are, facing the water.

paras.t: Look around at all these strangers from everywhere, standing together by the old walls and going quiet for the same few seconds. That shared quiet may be the best thing Oia gives anyone.
